title: The Downfall of Shakespeare in the Park
author: Annie Levin
content:
![The Downfall of Shakespeare in the
Park](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-26-at-9.25.19
---PM.png)

For decades, the free outdoor summer performances put on by Manhattan's Public
Theater have been a pillar of New York City's cultural scene. The New York
Shakespeare Festival, now called Free Shakespeare in the Park, launched the
careers of Meryl Streep, James Earl Jones, and George C. Scott; many other
notable figures of the stage and the screen have appeared in its acclaimed
performances since it was launched in 1954 by the theater artist Joseph Papp.
Born to Russian Jewish immigrants in Brooklyn in 1921, Papp believed that live
theater should be as accessible as the public library. With a thirty-five-foot
trailer attached to a decommissioned sanitation truck, he and his company
brought Shakespeare to the people for free.

When he first rolled his trailer to Central Park's Turtle Pond, Papp could
hardly have imagined what the festival would become in 2026: the Blade
helicopters droning past as the festival's director of fundraising thanks
Citizens Bank and other corporate sponsors for their generous contributions;
productions like last summer's star-studded _Twelfth Night_ , which recast the
beloved comedy as a cartoonish spectacle, part Shen Yun Circus and part
Spongebob musical.

The first production in this summer's season was a bilingual _Romeo and
Juliet_ set at the US-Mexico border wall. No English supertitles were provided
for non-Spanish-speaking audience members, nor Spanish supertitles for the
non-English-speakers in the crowd. The star-crossed lovers code-switched in
and out of Spanish, as in: "For saints have hands that pilgrims' hands do
touch / And palm to palm the palmer _les da un beso_." The laugh lines in
Spanish elicited obligatory titters from perhaps a fifth of the audience. The
rest maintained a guilty, awkward silence.

Juliet's balcony scene was staged on a guard tower on the border wall. The
Montagues, a Spanish-speaking family of indigenous activists from the wrong
side of the wall, staged a campus-style "Abolish ICE" banner drop; the
Capulets were border guards, dressed like goose-stepping blackshirts.
Transposing contemporary politics onto Shakespeare can, in theory, offer a
fruitful way of reimagining the play, but the politics here were slapped on
and made little sense. The Montagues and Capulets are "two families, both
alike in dignity" battling over ancient grudges; the tragic deaths of the
young protagonists prompt them to recognize the meaninglessness of the rivalry
and reconcile. The new production's desperate bid for relevance generated an
incoherent statement with little relation to the text, turning a tragic love
story about fate, love, and destructive enmity into a black and white morality
tale.

> "The performance was just as disheartening."

The performance was just as disheartening, with actors stepping so hard on
their laugh lines and gesticulating so wildly that it was as though director
Saheem Ali believed the audience, while fully fluent in Spanish, was shaky in
its English**.** As is all too common in contemporary productions of
Shakespeare, lines not delivered with vaudeville clownishness were rushed
through as though**** they were**** barely understood by the actors
themselves. Melding children's pantomime with liberal resistance signifiers,
productions like this treat audiences like Sunday school classes full of
subliterate children. _Romeo and Juliet_ , like last summer's _Twelfth Night_
, dripped with condescension.

Another factor at work here is the perceived need to tailor theatrical
productions to the demands of social media. Juliet standing on the US-Mexico
wall makes little sense, but it looks great on Instagram. In 2025's _Twelfth
Night_ , also directed by Ali, a huge portion of the budget was spent on _Drag
Rac_ e-themed costumes that were exclusively used for the __[_curtain
call_](https://www.tiktok.com/@oliviamazyuk/video/7550110665613069598?is_from_webapp=1&sender_device=pc&ref=compactmag.com)--a
wild made-for-TikTok extravaganza. The audience was encouraged to feel that it
was at a party with Peter Dinklage and Sandra Oh and all its parasocial
celebrity friends. Aren't you having fun? It asked. Isn't this the best time
ever? And if not, what's wrong with you?

 _Romeo and Juliet_ ended in a real live wedding ceremony, officiated by Friar
Laurence wearing an indigenous feathered cassock. Following the curtain call,
the friar, having just sent two beautiful teens to early graves, invites a
real couple on stage and actually marries them beneath Juliet's balcony/guard
tower. When I saw the play, the real-life bride and groom, possibly theater
donors, looked like they had just strolled down the stoop of their Park Slope
brownstone. The contrast with the young, non-white Romeo and Juliet, performed
by Daniel Bravo Hernandez and Ra'mya Latiah Aikens, was stark. On the one
hand, the exoticized fantasy of young love at the border wall; on the other,
the stone-faced bourgeois paying for the evening's entertainment.

The arts have almost always struggled under market conditions, but today's
most successful nonprofit theaters are subsumed in the nonprofit industrial
complex. The Public, which sponsors Shakespeare in the Park, is a massive
fundraising operation with bloated administrative costs; its artistic
director, [_Oskar Eustis_](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/22/theater/oskar-
eustis-public-theater.html?ref=compactmag.com), receives a salary of almost a
million dollars a year, even as the actors had to
[_fight_](https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2016/nov/14/off-broadway-fair-
wages-actors-equity-pay-minimum?ref=compactmag.com) through their union just
to gross about a thousand dollars a week.

Where today's theater artists beg and scrape before the donor class, Papp made
demands and didn't relent. He went toe-to-toe with [_Robert
Moses_](https://wnyc.org/story/44469-the-taming-of-robert-
moses/?ref=compactmag.com), the famously powerful New York Parks Commissioner,
to keep his plays free and open to the public. He
[_canceled_](https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-
xpm-1991-11-01-mn-582-story.html?ref=compactmag.com) a $7 million contract
with CBS when the network balked at airing his production of an anti-Vietnam
War drama, _Sticks and Bones._ It's hard to imagine today's well-paid artistic
directors acting similarly.

Today even Broadway is going bust, with Andrew Lloyd Webber's __[__Cats: The
Jellicle Ball__](https://variety.com/2026/legit/news/cats-the-jellicle-ball-
ending-broadway-run-early-1236810127/?ref=compactmag.com) closing despite
grossing almost a million a week. To survive but also to put an end to the
tawdry spectacle of liberal resistance Shakespeare, theater for the people
should be funded by the people. A**** government intervention on a scale not
seen since the New Deal is needed to make the arts thrive again. Until such
time, however, we also need a new generation of Joseph Papps: theater artists
with spine and a ferocious devotion to bringing art to the people.
